full_text_en:
Shanghai Huijun Logistics Co., Ltd. v. Ping An Property & Casualty Insurance Company of China, Ltd., Shanghai Branch, et al. — dispute over property insurance contract

Case Summary

In determining the true expression of intent formed by the final consensus of the parties to an insurance contract, a comprehensive judgment shall be made based on the constituent contents of the insurance contract, including the proposal form, insurance policy or other insurance certificates, and insurance clauses. Contract contents that are lawfully incorporated into the contract and have taken effect are legally binding on all parties to the insurance contract. Where a party asserts its rights under the insurance contract based solely on a unilateral expression of intent that did not form a final consensus during the contracting process, the people's court shall not support such claim.

Plaintiff: Shanghai Huijun Logistics Co., Ltd., domiciled at Lizheng Road, Shuyuan Town, Pudong New Area, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Wu Huilong, Executive Director of the Company.

Defendant: Ping An Property & Casualty Insurance Company of China, Ltd., Shanghai Branch, domiciled at Changshu Road, Jing'an District, Shanghai.
Person in Charge: Chen Xuesong, General Manager of the Branch.

Defendant: Ping An Property & Casualty Insurance Company of China, Ltd., domiciled at Yitian Road, Futian District, Shenzhen, Guangdong Province.
Legal Representative: Sun Jianping.

Plaintiff Shanghai Huijun Logistics Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huijun Logistics) initiated an action against Defendant Ping An Property & Casualty Insurance Company of China, Ltd., Shanghai Branch (hereinafter referred to as Ping An Property Shanghai Branch) and Defendant Ping An Property & Casualty Insurance Company of China, Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ping An Property Company) regarding a dispute over a property insurance contract, and filed the lawsuit with the Shanghai Jing'an District People's Court.

Plaintiff's Allegations: On March 30, 2018, the Plaintiff purchased Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance from the Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch, with the Plaintiff as the insured, for the period from March 31, 2018 to March 30, 2019. During the insurance period, a vehicle bearing license plate Hebei JU9550 was involved in a traffic accident while transporting goods for the Plaintiff, causing damage to the goods being carried by the Plaintiff. The Defendants refused to pay compensation on the grounds that the license plate number of the involved vehicle was not recorded in the insurance policy and that the Plaintiff had not declared the information of the accident vehicle to the Defendants. Therefore, the Plaintiff initiated this lawsuit, requesting the court to order the two Defendants to pay the Plaintiff insurance proceeds of RMB 1,832,944.20 (comprising cargo loss of RMB 1,828,444.20 and inspection fees of RMB 4,500), and to pay interest losses of RMB 1,988,758 (calculated from June 9, 2018 to August 19, 2019 at the benchmark loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China for the corresponding period, and from August 20, 2019 until the actual date of payment by the Defendants at the loan prime rate published by the National Interbank Funding Center).

Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch's Defense: The Defendant disagreed with all of the Plaintiff's claims. First, the vehicle involved in the accident was not owned by the Plaintiff, and the Plaintiff failed to declare the vehicle's information to the Defendant as required by the special stipulations of the insurance policy; therefore, the transported goods were not within the scope of the Defendant's coverage, and the Defendant had the right to refuse compensation. Second, even if the Defendant were liable for claims, a 20% deductible and the residual value of the goods should be deducted, and the Defendant did not agree to bear the appraisal fees incurred by the Plaintiff's unilateral engagement of a surveyor; the Plaintiff's claim for interest losses also lacked legal basis.

Facts Found by the Court at First Instance (Shanghai Jing'an District People's Court):

On March 30, 2018, Plaintiff Huijun Logistics purchased Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance from Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch, with the Plaintiff as the insured, for the period from March 31, 2018 to March 30, 2019. The Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Clauses stipulated: "During the insurance period, if the insured, in the course of operating its logistics business, suffers loss of or damage to the logistics goods themselves due to any of the following reasons, [...] the insurer shall be liable for compensation in accordance with the provisions of this insurance contract: [...] (2) Collision, derailment, overturning of transport vehicles, [...]" Special Stipulations No. 25 and 26 of the Insurance Policy stated: "This policy only covers the insurance liability for accidents involving the following listed carrier vehicles: If the insured needs to replace a carrier vehicle during the insurance period, it must declare the license plate number of the replacement carrier vehicle to the insurer by email at least one working day in advance; otherwise, the insurer shall not bear any insurance liability. Vehicle license plates: Shanghai BK4049; Shanghai BK4149; Shanghai EG9626; Shanghai EG1835; Shanghai EK5116; Shanghai EK5135; Shanghai ET2383; Shanghai EK1396." The "Special Stipulations" section of the Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Proposal Form stated "As per agreement." The "Insured's Declaration" section of the Proposal Form stated: "Your company has provided me with a detailed introduction to the contents of the Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Clauses and the various notes, explanations, and insurance instructions in this application form, and has specifically provided a clear explanation of the provisions regarding insurance coverage, exclusions, and the obligations of the insured and the policyholder. I accept the above contents and agree to apply for this insurance." The Plaintiff affixed its seal to this Proposal Form.

On June 8, 2018, a heavy semi-trailer towing vehicle bearing license plate Hebei JU9550 was involved in a traffic accident while transporting goods, causing damage to the goods being carried by Plaintiff Huijun Logistics. The Second Expressway Brigade of the Lianyungang City Traffic Police Detachment in Jiangsu Province determined that the driver of the accident vehicle bore full responsibility for the accident. After the Plaintiff reported the accident to Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch, the Defendant dispatched a surveyor on June 21 of the same year to conduct an inspection and confirm the quantity of damaged goods. On September 17 of the same year, the Defendant issued a Notice of Refusal of Claim to the Plaintiff, on the grounds that the accident vehicle had not been declared to the Defendant and the insurance liability was not established. On November 24 of the same year, the Plaintiff commissioned a third party, Renxiang Insurance Surveyors and Loss Adjusters (Beijing) Co., Ltd., to assess the loss of the aforementioned goods. The company assessed the loss amount at RMB 1,951,533.68 and the negotiated settlement amount at RMB 1,828,444.32, for which the Plaintiff paid an appraisal fee of RMB 4,500. During the trial, the Plaintiff and Ping An Property Shanghai Branch confirmed the amount of cargo loss as RMB 1,828,444.20 (without deducting the residual value of the goods). On April 28, 2020, Schenker (China) Co., Ltd. issued a compensation certificate, certifying that the negotiated settlement amount for the said cargo loss had been deducted from the Plaintiff's freight charges in 12 installments, and the deduction had been completed.

It was also found that during the negotiation process between the parties, on March 22, 2018, Plaintiff Huijun Logistics sent to an employee of Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch (now resigned) via WeChat the "Domestic Cargo Transportation Insurance Agreement of the People's Insurance Company of China" and the "Domestic Waterway, Land Cargo Transportation Insurance Clauses (2009 Version)." The employee informed the Plaintiff that this type of insurance was cargo transportation insurance. On March 29 and March 30 of the same year, the Defendant sent an email to the Plaintiff, including an attachment "Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Proposal Form," which stated: "The underwriting conditions are consistent with the previous PICC. Please review, Mr. Wu. Additionally, the following materials are required: 1. A photocopy of the business license stamped with the official seal. 2. A list of vehicles under the name of Shanghai Huijun Logistics Co., Ltd. (license plate numbers are sufficient) stamped with the official seal." Subsequently, the Plaintiff stamped the above materials and delivered them to Ping An Property Shanghai Branch. The "Transport Vehicles" column of the Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Proposal Form indicated the vehicle type as "General Cargo" and quantity as "8." The eight license plate numbers in the List of Self-Owned Freight Vehicles were consistent with the license plate information recorded in the Special Stipulations section of the aforementioned insurance policy. After receiving the insurance policy, the Plaintiff inquired with the Defendant about the procedure for cancellation but did not submit a cancellation application.

Opinion of the Court at First Instance (Shanghai Jing'an District People's Court):

The disputed issue in this case is whether the two Defendants could refuse compensation on the grounds that the accident vehicle was not a covered vehicle listed in the insurance policy, or that Plaintiff Huijun Logistics failed to declare the replacement carrier vehicle to the Defendants in accordance with the agreed procedure.

The disputed insurance contract represented the true intentions of all parties and was lawful and valid; all parties should abide by it. First, regarding Plaintiff Huijun Logistics's claim that Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch promised underwriting conditions "consistent with PICC," the court held that, based on the contracting process of the insurance contract in question, records of emails and WeChat messages were part of the negotiation process between the parties. During this process, the possibility of other new offers being made could not be excluded; therefore, this could not be used to confirm the final consensus of the parties. For example, during the contracting process, when the Defendant's former employee received the "Domestic Cargo Transportation Insurance Agreement of the People's Insurance Company of China" sent by the Plaintiff, he immediately informed the Plaintiff that this type was cargo transportation insurance. However, the insurance formally applied for by the Plaintiff was logistics liability insurance, which were different types. The Plaintiff did not raise any objection after being informed by the Defendant and receiving the Proposal Form. Therefore, in this case, the Proposal Form in question should be understood as the final offer made. Ping An Property Shanghai Branch agreed to underwrite the insurance, and the insurance contract was legally formed and took effect. In this case, the Proposal Form stated the quantity of general cargo transport vehicles as "8," and the List of Self-Owned Freight Vehicles also listed the license plate numbers of 8 vehicles under Huijun Logistics. These documents were stamped and confirmed by the Plaintiff before being submitted to the Defendant. The "Special Stipulations" section of the Proposal Form stated "As per agreement," and the Plaintiff stamped its seal in the "Insured's Declaration" section, confirming that the Defendant had provided a detailed introduction to the notes, explanations, and insurance instructions in the application form, and that the Plaintiff accepted the above contents and agreed to apply for insurance. Therefore, the Plaintiff's expression of intent was genuine and constituted an offer by the Plaintiff to the Defendant. The Defendant did not object to underwriting, so the insurance contract in this case was formed and was lawful and valid.

Second, the Insurance Policy, which recorded the agreed contents of the parties, had legal binding force. According to the contents of Special Stipulations No. 25 and 26 of the Insurance Policy, the insurance liability undertaken by Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch was limited to the 8 carrier vehicles listed in those stipulations. The license plate information of these vehicles was consistent with the List of Self-Owned Freight Vehicles submitted by Plaintiff Huijun Logistics, and the quantity of vehicles also matched the quantity of carrier vehicles stated in the List and the Proposal Form. Therefore, there was no inconsistency between the Proposal Form and the Insurance Policy in this case. The Plaintiff's reliance on Article 14 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China (II) lacked factual basis.

The Insurance Policy also stipulated that if Plaintiff Huijun Logistics needed to replace a carrier vehicle during the insurance period, it was required to declare the license plate number of the replacement carrier vehicle to Defendant Ping An Property Shanghai Branch at least one working day in advance; otherwise, the Defendant would not bear insurance liability. Special Stipulations No. 25 and 26 should be understood as special stipulations by the insurer to define the scope of insurance liability, and did not constitute exemption clauses. In this case, the accident vehicle was neither insured by the Defendant nor had the Plaintiff made an advance declaration as required by the Special Stipulations. Therefore, the Defendant's refusal to pay compensation was in accordance with the contract, and its relevant defense arguments were adopted. Third, although the Plaintiff claimed it had raised objections to the aforementioned Special Stipulations of the Insurance Policy, it did not submit a cancellation application to the Defendant. This could be deemed as the Plaintiff voluntarily accepting the binding effect of those Special Stipulations. In summary, the Plaintiff's claims lacked factual and legal basis and were not supported.

Judgment at First Instance:

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 60(1) of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 13 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 64(1) and Article 144 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Shanghai Jing'an District People's Court rendered its judgment on September 23, 2020:

All claims of Plaintiff Shanghai Huijun Logistics Co., Ltd. were dismissed.

Huijun Logistics, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai Financial Court, alleging:

1. The insurance application process in this case involved the Appellant contacting the insurance company via WeChat, explicitly requesting terms consistent with the PICC insurance. The Appellee Ping An Property Shanghai Branch replied by email that the insurance terms were consistent with PICC, but requested the Appellant to provide a list of its own vehicle license plates without explaining the purpose. Ultimately, only 8 trucks were insured. The Proposal Form provided by the Appellee was inconsistent with the final policy.
2. The Proposal Form was pre-formulated by the Appellee and constituted standard terms. There was only one signature block on the policy, which should be regarded as the Appellant's confirmation of the insurance type, premium, and term, not as an acknowledgment of understanding the content of the insurance contract terms. The Appellee failed to prove that it had fulfilled its duty to warn and explain the exclusion clauses.
3. Upon discovering the error in the policy, the Appellant immediately communicated with the Appellee. The fact that the Appellee sent a cancellation form also evidenced its remedial action for providing the erroneous policy.
4. In this case, the Proposal Form and the Insurance Policy were inconsistent. The Appellant had raised objections, and the Appellee failed to explain the discrepancy or obtain the Appellant's consent. Therefore, the rights and obligations of the parties should be determined based on the Proposal Form.

Appellee Ping An Property Shanghai Branch's Defense: The insurance contract was finalized after negotiation and communication between the parties. The Appellant Huijun Logistics's act of stamping and confirming the documents indicated its acknowledgment of the new expression of intent. The 8 vehicles listed in the policy were also provided by the Appellant itself. The provision in the insurance contract regarding the requirement for advance declaration when replacing vehicles to continue coverage was clear. The relevant exemption clauses were highlighted in bold and black type to warn the Appellant. Since the Appellee's staff delivered the cancellation procedures to the Appellant, but the Appellant ultimately did not actually cancel the policy, it should be deemed that the Appellant approved the insurance contract. The vehicle involved in the accident claimed by the Appellant had not been declared in advance, and its ownership did not belong to the Appellant. Therefore, the Appellee's refusal to compensate was not improper. In summary, the first-instance judgment was correct, and the Appellee requested the second-instance court to dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

Facts Found by the Court at Second Instance (Shanghai Financial Court):

The Shanghai Financial Court, upon second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found at first instance.

Opinion of the Court at Second Instance (Shanghai Financial Court):

Based on the existing evidence, the document to which Appellant Huijun Logistics affixed its official seal was the Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Proposal Form. This Proposal Form stipulated that the Proposal Form and the Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Clauses were both constituent parts of the insurance contract. The "Insured's Declaration" section of the Proposal Form stated that the insurer had provided a detailed introduction to the contents of the Ping An Logistics Liability Insurance Clauses and had specifically provided a clear explanation of the provisions on insurance coverage, exclusions, and the obligations of the insured and the policyholder. According to the facts found, the list of 8 self-owned vehicle license plates in the List of Self-Owned Freight Vehicles of Huijun Logistics was also provided by the Appellant after affixing its official seal.

Based on the contents of this Proposal Form, Appellee Ping An Property Shanghai Branch issued the Insurance Policy. Appellant Huijun Logistics claimed that during the negotiation process, the Appellee had made other stipulations regarding the insurance terms, but the evidence presented was insufficient to support this claim. Furthermore, even if, as the Appellant alleged, the Appellee had sent it materials concerning policy cancellation, the Appellant did not submit a clear and detailed cancellation application to the insurer. Accordingly, it should be determined that the rights and obligations of the Appellant and the Appellee should be based on the insurance policy finally signed by both parties. The Appellant's view that the rights and obligations of the parties should be determined based on the expressions made during the negotiation process was difficult to sustain.

According to the provisions of the Insurance Policy, if the insured needed to replace a carrier vehicle during the insurance period, it was required to declare the license plate number of the replacement carrier vehicle to the insurer by email at least one working day in advance; otherwise, the insurer would not bear any insurance liability. The vehicle involved in the Appellant Huijun Logistics's claim for insurance compensation was not among the 8 vehicles listed in the Appellant's provided List of Self-Owned Freight Vehicles, and the Appellant failed to adduce evidence that it had ever reported to Appellee Ping An Property Shanghai Branch that there would be a change in carrier vehicles. Therefore, the Appellee's refusal to compensate on the grounds that the license plate number of the accident vehicle did not comply with the insurance policy agreement between the parties was sustainable.

In conclusion, the appellate claims of Appellant Huijun Logistics were difficult to sustain and should be dismissed. The first-instance judgment was correct and should be affirmed.

Judgment at Second Instance:

Pursuant to Article 170(1)(1) and Article 175 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Shanghai Financial Court rendered its judgment on June 25, 2021:

The appeal was dismissed, and the original judgment was affirmed.
